title: The cloud of unknowing
hook: an old English guide says God can be reached by love, but never by thought

segments.voice: Yesterday, the pilgrim: a wanderer in a Russian story, trying to pray without ceasing. Your line was without ceasing. Did one short word or prayer keep coming back through your day? Day one thousand three hundred seventy-two.

Stop trying to figure God out. That instruction, more or less, sits at the heart of a small English book whose writer never signed it. The book opens with a warning: whoever holds it shouldn't pass it around to the merely curious, only to someone who means to give their whole life to the practice it describes. Then, a few chapters in, comes the instruction that sounds backwards for a book about God. Put your thinking down. Not because thinking is bad, the writer says, but because it can't reach that far. Something else can. Today's word is the picture the book draws to explain what stands in the way.
screen: `AN UNSIGNED BOOK, WITH A WARNING.` → `STOP TRYING TO FIGURE GOD OUT.` → `SOMETHING ELSE CAN REACH.`

segments.voice: The book is called The Cloud of Unknowing, and its picture works in two layers. Above you, between you and God, hangs a cloud of unknowing: dark, thick, and impossible to see through with the mind. Below you, the writer asks you to lay down a second cloud, a cloud of forgetting, and put under it everything else: your plans, your worries, even good thoughts about holy things. Then comes the center of the book. In chapter six an imagined student asks the obvious question: so how am I supposed to think about God? And the writer's answer, in plain paraphrase, is: I don't know. God can be loved, but not thought. By love God can be reached and held; by thought, never. So the job is not to clear the cloud. The job is to keep knocking on it, as the book puts it, with a sharp dart of longing love, and not to walk away whatever happens. The next chapter makes it practical. Take one short word, the writer says, a single syllable is best, like God or love. Fasten it to your heart. When thoughts crowd in and start explaining, answer every one of them with that word. The Bible has a picture like it, at the mountain in Exodus: "And the people stood afar off, and Moses drew near unto the thick darkness where God was." Not into light. Into thick darkness. Look back over this week and there is a thread. A Tibetan mantra, the desert monk's plain names for his thoughts, the Jesus Prayer, the pilgrim's one carried line: each hands a busy mind something small to hold. This little English book does something different with its word. It doesn't ride the breath. It's sent upward, like a knock, every time a thought gets in the way.
screen: `A CLOUD ABOVE, A CLOUD OF FORGETTING BELOW.` · `LOVED, BUT NOT THOUGHT.` · `A SHARP DART OF LONGING LOVE.` · `ONE WORD, FASTENED TO THE HEART.` · then, large: `MOSES DREW NEAR UNTO THE THICK DARKNESS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with one loving word. Settle, back upright, and let the breath slow. Choose a short word. If you pray, the book suggests God or love. If you don't, love works on its own, or any small word that points toward what you care about most. Don't tie it to the breath, the way yesterday's word was. Just hold it ready. When a thought arrives, a plan, a worry, a clever idea about this practice, don't argue with it. Answer it with the word, and let the thought slide under the cloud of forgetting. Then the word again. The bell holds the time.
The cloud of unknowing. The dark the mind can't see through, between the seeker and God, in an old English guide. The book's way through is love, aimed like a dart, not thought. Today's word.

Your line: by love, not thought. Today, when you catch yourself trying to solve something that won't be solved, a person, a loss, a big question, try one small act of love toward it instead. Day one thousand three hundred seventy-two.

howItsDone: Readers of The Cloud of Unknowing sit in silence with one short word, such as God or love, and return to it whenever thoughts arrive; the book is also a source for later Christian practices of silent prayer.

what a scholar hears: an unsigned English guide that pairs a cloud above with a cloud of forgetting below, and gives the reader one short word to hold.

notes: All Cloud of Unknowing material is paraphrased (no public-domain translation on the validator list; Underhill 1912 exists but wording was not checked). Confirm: prologue warning about who should read the book; cloud of forgetting (ch. 5); the student's question and 'God may be loved but not thought' (ch. 6); 'sharp dart of longing love' (ch. 6); the one-syllable word like God or love (ch. 7).

The book's anonymity is stated ('someone who never signed it'); no date or century is given in the script under the claims rule. The index hook's '14th-century' was left out; the script hook was softened to 'an old English guide'.
The link to Exodus 20:21 is presented as an older biblical picture, not as something the Cloud itself cites. Confirm the framing.
Week-end look-back names days 1366–1371 (Om mani padme hum, the teacher, the sand mandala, the desert, the Jesus Prayer, the pilgrim).

Editor: hook now opens on the instruction itself (varying a run of 'A [noun]...' scene openers) and drops the unsourced 'plenty of old books start that way'; 'the picture is older than the book' (a dating claim) became 'the Bible has a picture like it'; the week look-back now names only the days that really hand the mind something small to hold, and the teach and practice set the Cloud's word (a knock, answering each thought) apart from day 1371's breath-word practice.
